5411f681-9389-428b-a7f6-5caa977dedbc.name: Newtonian Mechanics for a Single Particle
5411f681-9389-428b-a7f6-5caa977dedbc.definition: The approach in classical mechanics where the position and velocity of a single point particle are known at an initial time, and all forces acting are modeled to determine future motion through equations of motion.
aliases: Newtonian Mechanics for a Single Particle

citations.snippet:
8.223 Lecture 1
In 8.01(2), you learned the Newtonian approach to classical mechanics (CM). For the simplest possible system
of a single point particle, you assume the position and velocity are known at some initial time and that all
forces acting on the particle can be modeled, then the equations of motion (EoM) tell the particle how to
update its motion, eﬀectively the EoM tell the particle where it will be and how it will be moving at all future
times. For example, Newton’s second law tells us the acceleration at any given time, the acceleration tells us
how to update the velocity, and the velocity tells us how to update the position. Newton’s picture, however,
makes no attempt to explain where Newton’s Laws come from or why quantities like energy, momentum, and

8.223 Lecture 3
In the previous two lectures, we saw that Newton’s Laws can be obtained from the following postulates:
(I) Inertial reference frames exist, and in any such frame the CoM of a system that experiences no external
interactions does not accelerate (Newton’s First Law).
(II) Space-time is homogeneous and isotropic, i.e. the fundamental laws of physics do not depend on the time,
or on the location and orientation in space.
We noted that these postulates are all about space-time itself, and have nothing to do with any speciﬁc
classical system or type of interaction.
Today we will see that Newton’s laws are not the only consequences of Postulates I and II. Recall that
if Postulate II holds (and it will for any isolated system), the Lagrangian cannot be an explicit function of
time.

75fc82f8-08c3-4c3e-a81b-b70170bee1e7.definition: Classical Mechanics (CM) is an effective theory valid within certain regions, such as where spacetime postulates hold, but it breaks down in extreme conditions like near black holes.

citations.snippet:
global homogeneity, isotropy, and inertial frames need not exist at all, though they remain excellent local
approximations except in extreme cases such as near a black hole. We will see some explicit examples of this
breaking later in the course. For now, we will focus on how these space-time postulates give rise to all of CM.

1854f6e0-5225-401b-ac40-e7ed7bb91448.name: Postulates of Classical Mechanics Reformulated via Space-Time Properties
1854f6e0-5225-401b-ac40-e7ed7bb91448.definition: The reformulation of classical mechanics on the basis of postulates stating the existence of inertial reference frames where non-accelerating center of mass motion occurs without external forces, and the homogeneity and isotropy of space-time, meaning fundamental physical laws do not depend on time or spatial location/orientation.
aliases: Postulates of Classical Mechanics Reformulated via Space-Time Properties

citations.snippet:
8.223 Lecture 2
In the previous lecture, we stated that in this course, classical mechanics (CM) is reformulated as a theory
based entirely on the following postulates:
(I) Inertial reference frames exist, and in any such frame the CoM of a system that experiences no external
interactions does not accelerate (Newton’s First Law).
(II) Space-time is homogeneous and isotropic, i.e. the fundamental laws of physics do not depend on the time,
or on the location and orientation in space.
We noted that these postulates are all about space-time itself, and have nothing to do with any speciﬁc
classical system or type of interaction. We also stated that based on these two space-time properties, our
goal is to derive Newton’s laws, conservation of energy, momentum, angular momentum, etc.—all of 8.01!

a4456686-2ef7-4284-b25a-9787c5f4d5b7.definition: If the Lagrangian is not explicitly dependent on time (due to time translation symmetry), the quantity E = Σ_i (∂L/∂q̇_i)q̇_i - L is conserved, commonly called energy.

citations.snippet:
8.223 Lecture 3
In the previous two lectures, we saw that Newton’s Laws can be obtained from the following postulates:
(I) Inertial reference frames exist, and in any such frame the CoM of a system that experiences no external
interactions does not accelerate (Newton’s First Law).
(II) Space-time is homogeneous and isotropic, i.e. the fundamental laws of physics do not depend on the time,
or on the location and orientation in space.
We noted that these postulates are all about space-time itself, and have nothing to do with any speciﬁc
classical system or type of interaction.
Today we will see that Newton’s laws are not the only consequences of Postulates I and II. Recall that
if Postulate II holds (and it will for any isolated system), the Lagrangian cannot be an explicit function of
time.

In the previous two lectures, we saw that Newton’s Laws can be obtained from the following postulates:
(I) Inertial reference frames exist, and in any such frame the CoM of a system that experiences no external
interactions does not accelerate (Newton’s First Law).
(II) Space-time is homogeneous and isotropic, i.e. the fundamental laws of physics do not depend on the time,
or on the location and orientation in space.
We noted that these postulates are all about space-time itself, and have nothing to do with any speciﬁc
classical system or type of interaction.
Today we will see that Newton’s laws are not the only consequences of Postulates I and II. Recall that
if Postulate II holds (and it will for any isolated system), the Lagrangian cannot be an explicit function of
time.

citations.snippet:
8.223 Lecture 4
Today we will look at how to use the Lagrangian formalism in non-inertial frames. We will see that dealing
with non-inertial frames is much easier here than in 8.01.
Let’s start by considering a point particle in 2-D whose position in a non-inertial frame is (x, y), where
this frame is traveling with non-constant velocity⃗V (t) = V (t)ˆx relative to an inertial frame. We derived the
Lagrangian formalism in inertial frames, and indeed their existence and their equivalence of validity was one
of our postulates, hence it should not be surprising that we need to write the kinetic and potential terms
in the Lagrangian as they would be evaluated by somebody in an inertial frame. We can do this, however,
using coordinates from the non-inertial frame:
L = 1
2m| ˙⃗x +⃗V (t)|2 −U,

This lecture is about normal modes, which you will be familiar with if you have taken 8.03, and likely
unfamiliar with if you have not. This lecture will ﬁrst introduce what normal modes are, for those who
have not had 8.03, and then show how we can obtain them when studying oscillatory systems using the
Lagrangian formalism.

at a ﬁxed frequency. These frequencies are known as the natural frequencies or resonant frequencies of a
system. The most general motion of a linear

172f795b-46c1-41ff-aa32-3b07548f9c25.name: Infrared Radiation Emission Altitude
172f795b-46c1-41ff-aa32-3b07548f9c25.definition: The effective altitude in the atmosphere above which the atmosphere becomes transparent to a particular infrared wavelength, determining where radiation escapes to space.

citations.snippet:
important to emphasize that CO2 does not warm the planet by simply trapping infrared radiation
near the surface. For the strongest CO2 bands, the atmosphere was already optically thick long before
modern increases in concentration, so most infrared photons in those wavelength ranges are absorbed and
re-emitted many times regardless of recent CO2 levels. What matters instead is where in the atmosphere
radiation ﬁnally escapes to space. Each infrared wavelength has an eﬀective emission altitude deﬁned by the
condition that the atmosphere becomes transparent above it. Because temperature decreases with height
in the troposphere, radiation emitted from higher altitudes comes from colder air and therefore carries less
power, according to the blackbody law.

21f42b2d-bddd-488f-ae7b-0bf731f80648.name: Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion
21f42b2d-bddd-488f-ae7b-0bf731f80648.definition: Three empirical laws describing the motion of planets: 1) Planets move in ellipses with the Sun at a focus; 2) The line joining a planet and the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal times; 3) The square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis of its orbit.

This lecture is the start of a three-lecture journey exploring gravitational systems. Unlike in 8.01, we will
not assume all orbits are circular, and instead will fully solve the general 2-body orbital problem. We will
also derive all 3 of Kepler’s Laws from Newton’s law of gravity.

gravitation. Kepler spent years deriving his laws empirically, i.e. he had no underlying theory, instead he
analyzed observational data of the orbits of the planets in our solar system and was able to work out a set
of rules that all of these orbits obeyed, though he had no explanation as to why they did so. Kepler’s laws:

b251b201-90d1-4b72-90c2-e59275f8364a.name: Orbital Path Equation in Two-Body Problem
b251b201-90d1-4b72-90c2-e59275f8364a.definition: The formula r(θ) = α / (1 + ε cos θ) describes the orbital separation between two masses in a two-body system, where α and ε are constants and ε < 1 for bound orbits.
aliases: Orbital Path Equation in Two-Body Problem

In the previous lecture, we derived all 3 of Kepler’s Laws from Newton’s law of gravitation. A major result
was that orbital paths are given by
r(θ) =

8e644dc9-0e4b-4b55-a968-f6c565c22f2e.name: Constraint Equation in Mechanical Systems
8e644dc9-0e4b-4b55-a968-f6c565c22f2e.definition: An equation fk(qi, t) = 0 expressing known relationships between coordinates qi and time t in a system, restricting its motion.

citations.snippet:
8.223 Lecture 9
Consider a system described by nq coordinates qi but with nc known relationships between those coordinates,
which can be expressed as constraint equations in the form fk(qi, t) = 0. Thus far in this class, we have
ﬁrst solved the constraint equations to simply reduce the number of coordinates we used in the problem
to nq −nc. We have done this implicitly, e.g., when using the rolls without slipping constraint, we have
expressed the location of a rolling object in terms of how much it has rotated, rather than introducing a
dedicated coordinate for its location. It is important to note that what we have been doing gives the correct
results because none of the constraint forces we have implicitly implemented by reducing the number of
coordinates has done any work on the system

swing in 2-D; however, a motor is connected to the pivot point which causes the 2-D plane in which
the pendulum swings to rotate about the vertical axis with a constant angular frequency ω. Label the
angle of the pendulum from the vertical axis θ.
a) Write the Lagrangian for this system and ﬁnd the equation of motion for θ. [10 pts]
b) Which term in the EoM arises due to a ﬁctitious force when the pendulum is studied from a
co-rotating frame, i.e. a frame that also rotates about the vertical axis with frequency ω? [5 pts]

citations.snippet:
1. A point particle with mass m is constrained to move in 2-D (the x-y plane) in the presence of a potential
U(x, y) = k
2(x2 + y2) + αxy, where k, α are positive constants with k > α.
a) Write the Lagrangian and ﬁnd the equations of motion for coordinates x, y. [10 pts]
b) Find the Hamiltonian, H(x, y, px, py) and specify whether H is conserved (justify your answer). [5 pts]
c) Label the angular momentum about the origin⃗ℓ, and show that it is, in general (for any x, y), only
conserved if α = 0 using the following: [15 pts]
(i) a Newtonian approach based on how the force due to U aﬀects⃗ℓ;
(ii) a Canonical approach using Poisson Brackets and that dℓ/dt = [ℓ, H];
(iii) and a Noether-based approach where ℓis the conjugate momentum to a coordinate you must deﬁne,
then use Noether’s Theorem t
